result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.random_spanning_tree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Draw a random spanning tree of a connected undirected graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L61238-L61334){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.random_spanning_tree( weighted=None, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Random spanning tree](/assets/graphs/random-spanning-tree.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a 4 by 4 grid graph, 16 nodes and 24 edges. Right: the spanning tree drawn with seed 7, its 15 edges in the accent color and the 9 unused grid edges dashed. Every node is reached by exactly one route, so the tree reads as a maze." width="100%"} Every spanning tree is equally likely on an unweighted graph. On a weighted graph (or with `weighted=True`), a tree is chosen with probability proportional to the product of its edge weights, so heavier edges are more likely to appear. Random spanning trees are used to generate random mazes, to build sparse random backbones of a network, in Monte Carlo estimates of network reliability, and as a null model for tree-shaped data. Self-loops are never chosen, and edges with weight zero are never chosen. Among parallel edges, each is a separate candidate. The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to draw trees in proportion to the product of their edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Seed for the random number generator, for reproducible results. If `None` (default), a fresh random tree is drawn on each call. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected graph with every node of the original (IDs, labels and attributes kept) and the `n - 1` tree edges (weights and attributes copied). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed, empty, disconnected (counting only positive-weight edges when weighted), or has a negative weight. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Wilson's algorithm (1996) grows the tree from a random root. From each node not yet in the tree it runs a random walk until the walk hits the tree, erases the loops of that walk, and grafts the remaining path onto the tree. With walks that step along an edge with probability proportional to its weight, the result follows the weighted uniform spanning tree distribution exactly, $P(T) \propto \prod_{e \in T} w(e)$. The expected running time is the mean hitting time of the random walk, which is close to linear for well-connected graphs. NetworkX also offers an additive (sum of weights) distribution, which is not supported here. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Random spanning trees of a grid are mazes: every cell is reachable from every other by exactly one route. ::: {#1a1f12d7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec grid = ec.Graph().add_grid_2d(4, 4) maze = grid.random_spanning_tree(seed=7) maze.count_edges(), maze.is_tree() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (15, True) ``` ::: ::: The same seed gives the same tree: ::: {#2c47e2f1 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} again = grid.random_spanning_tree(seed=7) sorted(maze.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True)) == sorted( again.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: ::: On a weighted triangle, the tree that leaves out the light edge has weight `4 * 4 = 16` against `4 * 1 = 4` for each of the others, so it is drawn about two thirds of the time: ::: {#9cc44b5b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} tri = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) tri.add_edges([("A", "B", 4.0), ("B", "C", 4.0), ("C", "A", 1.0)]) draws = [tri.random_spanning_tree(seed=s) for s in range(3000)] sum(t.find_edge_ids("C", "A") == [] for t in draws) / 3000 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0.6526666666666666 ``` ::: :::
